messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: eQTL
parts:
It is, in that expression phenotypes may be treated like any other
phenotype.
In the next release of R/qtl, scanone() and scantwo() can consider
multiple
phenotypes at once, by either Haley-Knott or imputation; this gives
great
improvement in speed, which will be useful for those interested in
mapping
with thousands of phenotypes.

karl

messages.author: 59ddd620b9f8604d
messages.subject: Re: eQTL
parts:
Hi, Karl:
Thanks!
One question about eQTL is : because we consider over 20000 probes at
the same time, we have lots of penalties because of the multiple
testing problem. How does R/QTL handle this? Also, currently published
papers on eQTL majorly involve RI strains, and with very small sample
size. For instance , if we have 15 RI strains, with 3 arrays for each
strain, we only have 45 sample for each probe. Then how much power we
have to detect an eQTL ?
Sabrina

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: eQTL
parts:
Good points, both.

We don't have any specific facilities for accounting for the
enormous number of tests in such analyses.

Regarding power for the case of 15 strains with 3 arrays each:
not much. I view this task as exploratory, and wouldn't be rigid
about statistical significance.

karl

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: eQTL
parts:
It's no doubt possible to compute FDR, but I've not studied it and
can't suggest how to do it.

How many strains are needed...as always, it depends on the truth
and your goals.

R/qtl can handle RILs, but it's not yet documented. When you read
in your data with read.cross(), you want to use the argument
genotypes=c("AA","BB") or however the two homozygotes are coded.
Then, once the data have been read, they should appear as a
backcross. To change the cross type to RIL, use

class(mycross)[1] <- "risib"

or "riself" for RILs by selfing.

The data will be treated like a backcross, but expanding the genetic
map appropriately.

karl
